Building from source
********************


Building the crates
===================

Rust 1.88 or newer is required.

   git clone https://github.com/gtfierro/ontoenv-rs
   cd ontoenv-rs

   cargo build -p ontoenv-cli --release
   ./target/release/ontoenv --help

   cargo test

The workspace holds four crates:

"lib"
   "ontoenv" — the core environment, import resolution, and dependency
   graph.

"cli"
   "ontoenv-cli" — the command-line front end.

"python"
   The PyO3 bindings published to PyPI as "ontoenv".

"rdf5d"
   The on-disk RDF format used for graph storage and the metadata
   catalog.


Building the Python bindings
============================

Python 3.11 or newer.

   cd python
   uv run maturin develop

   uv run pytest


Building the docs
=================

The documentation has its own "pyproject.toml" under "docs/" so its
tooling stays separate from the project’s.

   ./builddocs          # sync deps, build the extension, render HTML
   ./builddocs llms     # also render docs/_build/llms.txt for LLM ingestion

Or by hand:

   cd docs
   uv sync
   uv run sphinx-build -M html . _build
   open _build/html/index.html


How the docs are organized
==========================

The structure follows Diátaxis. When adding a page, put it in the
section matching what the reader is doing:

"tutorials/"
   Learning. A guaranteed-to-work path through a task, for someone who
   has not used OntoEnv before. No alternatives, no caveats, no edge
   cases.

"how-to/"
   Working. One page per goal, assuming competence. Terse; link out
   for background rather than explaining inline.

"reference/"
   Looking things up. Complete, dry, and organized by the shape of the
   API rather than by task. Tables over prose.

"explanation/"
   Understanding. Why things are the way they are. This is where
   design rationale, trade-offs, and edge cases belong — keep them out
   of the other three.

The most common mistake is letting explanation leak into a how-to, or
reference detail into a tutorial. If a paragraph starts with “note
that” or “the reason for this is”, it probably belongs in
"explanation/".


How the docs should sound
=========================

Write for a reader who has a real ontology and wants to know what
OntoEnv will do with it. Start with the useful fact, command, or
decision. Introduce the underlying model once the reader has something
concrete to attach it to.

Across all four sections:

* Prefer short paragraphs with one claim each.

* Use concrete verbs. Say that a command scans files, downloads an
  ontology, writes configuration, or deletes an environment.

* Show the result of an important command, not just the command
  itself.

* Introduce each command with the operation it performs. When a block
  contains several commands, say whether they are alternatives or a
  sequence, and describe the state changed by each step.

* State defaults, persistence, network access, mutation, and failure
  behavior when they could change a reader’s decision.

* Keep examples internally consistent and small enough to understand
  in one sitting.

* Do not call a task simple or easy. Show the shortest reliable path
  instead.

* Distinguish guarantees from advice. Use “does” for behavior and “we
  recommend” for a judgment.

* Avoid slogans, superlatives, and unqualified comparisons. Replace
  claims such as “fast”, “powerful”, or “covers most uses” with a
  mechanism, a measurement, or nothing.

* Do not advertise OntoEnv to the reader. Describe the problem it
  addresses, its behavior, and its limits; let the reader decide
  whether it fits.

The four sections use the same plain language for different ends:

"tutorials/"
   Move through a working example. After each important step, show
   enough output for the reader to confirm that they are on track.

"how-to/"
   Put the canonical command or code first. Then cover verification
   and the failure cases a competent user is likely to meet.

"reference/"
   Use a predictable order: signature, behavior, arguments, return
   value, side effects, errors, example, and related operations. Omit
   headings that genuinely do not apply.

"explanation/"
   Name the design question, the constraints, the choice OntoEnv
   makes, and the consequences of that choice. Be direct about costs
   and limitations.


Publishing documentation versions
=================================

The documentation site keeps each release at "/versions/<tag>/" and
the current main branch at "/dev/". The site root shows the newest
stable release once stable documentation has been published.
Publishing a prerelease or updating development docs preserves
existing release versions and the stable root. The sidebar selector
identifies prerelease and development documentation and links to every
published version.

To publish or rebuild documentation for an existing release, run the
"Deploy docs to Pages" workflow on "main" with "version_tag" set to
the release tag, for example "v0.7.0-rc.1". The workflow checks out
that tag for the documentation and Python bindings while using the
current deployment tools. Leave "version_tag" empty to publish
development documentation.

The workflow stores the complete site on "gh-pages" so subsequent
builds can preserve earlier versions. GitHub Pages uses the uploaded
site artifact; do not change Pages to build directly from a source
branch.
Concepts
********


Ontologies are identified by IRI, not by location
=================================================

An RDF ontology declares its own name:

   <https://example.org/site> a owl:Ontology .

That IRI is the ontology’s identity. It is not a URL you are promised
to be able to fetch, and it need not resemble the path of the file
containing it. Two copies of the same ontology in different
directories declare the same IRI; a file renamed on disk still
declares the same IRI.

Imports are written in the same currency:

   <https://example.org/site> owl:imports <https://example.org/sensors> .

This says *what* is needed, not *where* it is. Something has to close
that gap, and that something is what OntoEnv is.


An environment is a name-to-location index
==========================================

An environment is a directory — ".ontoenv-snapshots/" for managed
storage — holding two things:

**The graphs themselves**, in a compact binary format (rdf5d) that can
be memory-mapped and read without parsing RDF text.

**A catalog** describing them: for each ontology, its canonical IRI,
where it came from, any aliases, its namespace prefixes, and its
"owl:imports" targets.

The catalog is the interesting half. Because it records the import
relationships explicitly, OntoEnv can answer “what does this ontology
need?” by walking a graph in memory, rather than by re-parsing files.
It is also small — it holds facts *about* ontologies, not their
triples — which is why reopening an environment takes about the same
time whether it holds a thousand triples or a million.


Discovery: how ontologies get in
================================

Three routes:

* "init <dir>" / "search_directories=" — walk a directory, parse every
  file matching the include filters, record the IRI each one declares.

* "add <path-or-url>" — register one ontology, then follow its
  "owl:imports" and register those too, recursively.

* "update()" — revisit sources already known to the environment and
  re-read the ones that changed.

Remote ontologies are fetched over HTTP and cached on disk with a TTL,
so the second run of a program does not re-download anything.


Closures
========

The transitive closure of an ontology is that ontology plus everything
it imports, plus everything *those* import, and so on. It is the set
of graphs you need in order to interpret the first one.

OntoEnv does not hand you a raw concatenation of that set. A closure
is *flattened*:

* **Resolved ``owl:imports`` statements are removed.** They have
  already been followed. Leaving them in invites a downstream consumer
  to follow them again — probably over the network, probably to a
  different version.

* **Ontology declarations are collapsed onto the root.** A merged
  graph with twelve "owl:Ontology" subjects is ambiguous about what it
  *is*. The result declares one ontology: the root you asked for.

* **SHACL prefix declarations are consolidated** onto the root, so
  "sh:prefixes" still resolves in the merged graph.

* **Duplicate triples appear once.**

The result is a single self-contained graph. That is usually what you
want when handing a closure to a reasoner, a validator, or a
colleague.

When you want the other thing — exactly the graphs you named,
untouched — that is a **union**: "ontoenv union" /
"env.get_union(...)". Unions do not strip imports, do not collapse
declarations, and do not de-duplicate across graphs.


Aliases and canonical IRIs
==========================

Real ontologies get published at more than one IRI: with and without a
version suffix, over "http" and "https", at a vanity domain and a
permanent one. An alias maps an extra IRI onto an ontology already in
the environment.

An alias may only point at a canonical IRI, never at another alias —
so resolution is always a single hop and chains cannot form. Aliases
resolve transparently everywhere an IRI is accepted.


Resolution policy
=================

Managed storage keeps one registration per canonical IRI. When an
explicit add encounters an IRI already in the catalog, its overwrite
option controls whether the existing registration is preserved or
replaced. Replacement changes the source/contents together and
preserves explicit aliases. It does not retain multiple source
versions for later policy selection.

The "resolution_policy" setting selects among multiple registrations
only where the catalog/backend can represent them, such as temporary
or external store catalogs:

"default"
   Prefer the first-registered definition.

"latest"
   Prefer the most recently updated source.

"version"
   Prefer the highest "owl:versionIRI" / version property.

These policies do not rank competing source files during managed
ingestion or override an explicit preserve/replace choice. For
reproducible managed builds, choose the intended source explicitly;
distinct versions that must coexist need distinct graph IRIs. Do not
depend on directory traversal order to select one. "ontoenv doctor"
can report duplicate registrations in catalogs that allow them.


Strict mode
===========

By default an unresolvable import is a warning: OntoEnv assembles what
it can and tells you what is missing. In strict mode it is an error.

Non-strict is the right default for exploration — a closure missing
one obscure vocabulary is usually still useful. Strict is the right
setting for CI, where silently incomplete output is worse than a
failure.


Persistent and temporary environments
=====================================

A persistent environment writes immutable versions under ".ontoenv-
snapshots/" and reopens quickly because of its saved catalog. A
temporary one ("--temporary" / "OntoEnv(temporary=True)") keeps graphs
and catalog in memory, leaves nothing behind, and starts from scratch
every time. The API is otherwise identical.

Use "env.snapshot()" for fixed read-only access to an existing managed
version. Its graph and dataset views retain that version after the
environment closes or another writer publishes. Use "copy_graph()" or
"copy_dataset()" for mutable data; changes to these copies do not
change the environment. To manage a separate in-memory collection,
create "OntoEnv(temporary=True)" and add the desired graph copies. A
temporary environment’s "root" is only a configuration base for source
paths; it does not load saved state.

Persistent environments allow one writer at a time. Any number of
readers can open the same environment read-only.

See also:

  Views and copies for what a closure gives you in Python, and Opening
  an environment for the ways to open an environment.
Atomic publication belongs to OntoEnv
*************************************

Status: 0.7.0-rc.1 preparation in PR #36, October 23, 2026. Immutable
manifests and an atomic "CURRENT" file are the default managed storage
in Rust, Python and the CLI. See the snapshot guide for APIs and
measurements.


The boundary
============

RDF5D is an immutable, queryable storage artifact. It owns encoding,
validation, file construction, mmap access, triple lookup and query
indexes. Its "Snapshot" is an owned query handle to fixed file
contents. Building query indexes lazily inside that handle does not
change the published file.

OntoEnv owns source discovery, ontology identity, aliases, imports,
configuration and publication of complete environment versions. Writer
exclusion, version numbers, commit timestamps, refresh and recovery
belong here. A version bundles the catalog and configuration with a
reference to an immutable RDF5D file. There is no independent catalog
save after graph publication.

+----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| Component                                          | Responsibility                                     |
|====================================================|====================================================|
| RDF5D                                              | Build, validate, open and query a fixed artifact   |
+----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| OntoEnv update                                     | Stage graph replacements/deletions and candidate   |
|                                                    | metadata                                           |
+----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| OntoEnv publication                                | Select one complete environment version atomically |
+----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| OntoEnv reader                                     | Retain one version until explicit refresh          |
+----------------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+

All publication code lives in "lib/src/snapshots.rs"; the RDF5D crate
gains no transaction machinery. The old Cargo feature name is an empty
compatibility feature; managed storage no longer requires opting in.


Minimal contract
================

For a local filesystem, one writer, roughly 100 graphs and 10–20 MB of
encoded data, with bursty writes and readers explicitly refreshing:

1. Published RDF5D objects and selected manifests never change in
   place.

2. One selected manifest identifies catalog, configuration and graph
   data as a unit. Readers do not assemble a version from
   independently current files or filesystem modification times.

3. Graph-changing commits write a complete new RDF5D artifact.
   Metadata-only commits reuse the previous artifact. Beginning an
   update clones small metadata and holds only graph
   replacements/deletions in an overlay.

4. Preparation is private. Abort, Drop, parse errors and validation
   failures do not publish. Successful publication has one authority
   change.

5. Readers do not hold the writer’s lock. Retained views keep their
   old mapping and metadata. Refresh validates a replacement before
   swapping it; a refresh error leaves the old view intact.

6. A publication I/O error may mean old or new head is durable.
   Further commits from that writer are rejected until close/reopen
   reconciles head. Its last confirmed snapshot remains readable but
   may be behind durable head.

7. Keep all complete objects and manifests initially. Neither retained
   files nor a generation counter promise a public history/checkout
   API. Reset publishes a replacement version. Migration is explicit
   and preserves legacy files. Online pruning is not supported.


Disk layout and authority
=========================

   root/
     .ontoenv-snapshots.lock      # stable exclusive writer lock
     .ontoenv-snapshots/
       CURRENT                   # schema, manifest file name, BLAKE3 of its bytes
       manifests/
         manifest-<unique>.json   # version info, catalog, config, object reference
       objects/
         object-<unique>/
           store.r5tu            # complete immutable RDF5D artifact

Pointer and manifest schemas are version 2. Names are validated as
restricted single path components before use. Random names avoid
collision with abandoned attempts; version numbers describe committed
versions rather than filenames. Readers follow only "CURRENT",
validate the selected manifest’s checksum/schema, then map exactly its
object. Missing/corrupt selected content is an error, not permission
to scan for another manifest. Objects retain RDF5D’s existing CRC
validation; the manifest checksum does not make external mutation of
mmap data safe.

Earlier redb-based experimental environments are rejected explicitly.
Neither those environments nor legacy ".ontoenv/" stores are
overwritten by normal open/create calls. Legacy managed stores have an
explicit copy migration. The specialized Rust reader/update API
remains available alongside the normal API.


Publication protocol
====================

1. Hold the stable writer lock. Prepare and validate the complete
   candidate.

2. If graphs changed, finish, validate and sync a unique RDF5D object
   and sync its containing directory entries. Metadata-only updates
   reuse the old object.

3. Check the expected environment identity/head under the writer lock.
   Write a unique manifest, sync its bytes, retain it, close it and
   sync "manifests/".

4. Write a small temporary pointer in the directory containing
   "CURRENT", naming that manifest and its BLAKE3 checksum. Sync its
   bytes and close the handle.

5. Atomically replace "CURRENT" using "std::fs::rename", then sync its
   parent directory. Replacement is the visibility point. No
   unlink/truncate of the old pointer occurs. Prepare the writer’s in-
   memory snapshot before this step so installing it afterward cannot
   fail through file I/O.

The expected-head check is not a compare-and-swap for processes
bypassing the stable writer lock. All cooperating writers must take
that lock. Initialization prepares version zero in a private sibling
directory, then renames the complete directory into place. The writer
lock remains outside that directory and is never replaced or removed.

A reader closes "CURRENT" and the manifest before mapping RDF5D. A
concurrent publication may mean it selects the previous version; that
is a valid coherent snapshot. Since nothing is pruned, both the
selected manifest and its object remain available without a lock
spanning selection and mapping. Fresh readers need no writer to repair
files after an abrupt process exit. Unreferenced files left by
interrupted attempts are ignored and retained.

The tempfile dependency creates unique pointer files and clears
temporary file attributes before the writing handle closes. Rust’s
"std::fs::rename" performs replacement without first unlinking
CURRENT. On Windows it has a POSIX-semantics fallback for replacing a
file whose readers still hold it open; tempfile’s MoveFileExW-only
persistence failed the concurrent-reader stress test. A regression
test now keeps the old CURRENT handle open throughout publication and
checks that it still reads the old bytes after new opens select the
new pointer. Rust 1.88 Windows implementation. Directory sync
currently runs on Unix and is a no-op elsewhere. Passing Windows
process tests establishes normal-operation/process-exit behavior, not
a Windows power-loss guarantee. Filesystem and device flush semantics
also matter on Unix. A bounded guest crash/reboot campaign has now
been performed on Linux/ext4; see validation and acceptance gates for
its results and limits. It does not power-cycle host or device caches.


Why replace the manifest database?
==================================

The mutable authority is one selected version. The earlier redb
prototype used experimental multiprocess support to coordinate this
small head. It also needed a writer to recover before a fresh read-
only open after an unclean writer exit. The file publisher removes
that availability dependency, database handles, internal history table
and redb’s higher compiler requirement. It keeps direct RDF5D mmap
access and does not introduce a public backend abstraction.

This is a simplicity/availability experiment, not a claim that files
are faster than a database. Two synced files and directory barriers
have a cost. The updated profile compares this implementation with the
saved redb baseline; neither is a controlled filesystem benchmark.
Whole-file rewrites, rather than query or codec changes, remain the
chosen starting point.


Acceptance coverage and remaining work
======================================

The Linux test suite covers explicit refresh and retained views,
writer exclusion, rollback, aliases/configuration, empty versus
removed graphs, source IRI changes, failed refresh, invalid CURRENT
paths/schema/checksum, invalid selected manifests, and explicit
rejection of earlier redb environments.

Child-process tests exit at eight points: object ready, manifest
written, manifest synced, manifest directory synced, pointer written,
pointer synced, pointer replaced, and final directory synced. At every
point a fresh reader opens before any recovery writer, selecting
exactly the old or new complete version. A new writer can then publish
immediately. Injected publication errors on either side of replacement
disable retry until reopen; known preparation failures allow retry.

A second test runs three reader processes opening and refreshing while
a writer publishes twenty successive changes. Each reader checks graph
content, aliases and configuration against its selected version and
retains its original view. Dedicated feature CI runs these tests on
Linux, macOS and Windows at Rust 1.88; consult the PR checks for
results on the current revision. The Windows fix and repeated stress
passed on all three platforms at "ac607d9".

Before normal Rust/Python/CLI integration, review platform durability
guarantees, measure cold reads and query-index memory across
processes, and add recursive source updates and explicit legacy
migration. Online cleanup requires a separate protocol covering
sleeping readers and every retained query view. Per-graph disk COW
remains deferred until complete-file publication measurements justify
changes to dictionary ownership and cross-graph queries.
Explanation
***********

Concepts
   Ontologies, IRIs, imports, closures, and the environment that ties
   them together. Read this first if the vocabulary is unfamiliar.

Views and copies
   Why every read method comes in a "get_*" and a "copy_*" flavour,
   what a closure view actually contains, and how to choose.

Namespaces and prefix precedence
   Where prefixes come from, which bindings win, and how to edit saved
   or local choices.

Opening an environment
   There are five ways to open an environment. What each one refuses
   to do, and why "connect" is almost always the right answer.

Staying in sync
   OntoEnv never reads your files behind your back. What "update()"
   and "refresh_from_store()" each reconcile, and why they are
   separate.

Performance
   Benchmarks against in-memory rdflib and Oxigraph, plus the indexing
   that explains the results.

OntoEnv publication and snapshots
   Default managed storage with immutable mmap-backed generations,
   concurrent readers, staged updates, and explicit snapshot refresh.

Atomic publication belongs to OntoEnv
   Why atomic publication belongs to OntoEnv, the RDF5D boundary, and
   the immutable-manifest publication protocol.

Publication validation and acceptance gates
   Platform results, guest crash/reboot tests, multi-process workloads
   and provisional acceptance budgets for the publisher.
Opening an environment
**********************


Use "connect" when either state is valid
========================================

   from ontoenv import OntoEnv

   env = OntoEnv.connect("./ontology-env")

"connect" is a class method with a required path;
"OntoEnv.connect(".")" uses the current directory. The returned handle
can live for the whole program.

"connect" creates the environment if it is missing and reopens it if
it exists. Use a different entry point when one of those states should
be an error.

The rest of this page is about the other five entry points, which
exist so a program can *refuse* the lifecycle states it does not
expect.

The design question is not how many constructors an environment needs.
It is which startup mistakes should stop the program immediately.

+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| Entry point              | Use when                               | If the environment already exists / is |
|                          |                                        | missing                                |
|==========================|========================================|========================================|
| "OntoEnv.connect(path)"  | Normal startup                         | Reopens it / creates it                |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| "OntoEnv.create(path)"   | Setup must create a new one            | Fails unless "overwrite=True" /        |
|                          |                                        | creates it                             |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| "OntoEnv.open(path)"     | Deployment already prepared it         | Opens it / fails                       |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| "OntoEnv.adopt(path,     | A custom store is already populated    | Fails unless "overwrite=True" /        |
| store)"                  |                                        | indexes the store                      |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| "OntoEnv.recover(path)"  | Startup raised "CatalogRecoveryError"  | Rebuilds the index from the graph      |
|                          |                                        | store                                  |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
| "OntoEnv(temporary=True  | Nothing should be saved                | Always a fresh in-memory environment   |
| )"                       |                                        |                                        |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+


Choose which assumption to enforce
==================================

"connect" accepts both an existing environment and a missing one.

If a missing environment is an error, accepting both states hides
useful information. If your deployment pipeline is supposed to have
built the environment, a process that silently creates an empty one
instead will start up fine and then behave as though every ontology
vanished. "OntoEnv.open(path)" fails during startup instead.

The same reasoning applies in reverse. A setup command or a test
fixture that means to create a *new* environment should not quietly
adopt whatever was left over from a previous run.
"OntoEnv.create(path)" fails instead, and "overwrite=True" says you
meant it.

Each named method turns an assumption into a startup check. Use one of
the specialized methods when violating its assumption should stop the
program:

* "open" requires an environment that was prepared already.

* "create" requires a path that is safe to initialize.

* "adopt" requires a populated external graph store.

* "recover" requires evidence of an interrupted catalog mutation.

Use "connect" when both “open the saved environment” and “this is the
first run” are valid outcomes.


Connect does not read your files
================================

"connect" and "update" perform separate operations:

   env = OntoEnv.connect("./ontology-env", search_directories=["./ontologies"])
   env.update()   # <- this is what reads ./ontologies

"connect" loads the saved catalog. "update" scans sources. A process
can therefore reopen an environment without scanning its RDF files.
Source content changes are not visible until "update" runs.

The first "connect" on a brand-new environment creates the directory,
saves settings, and initializes empty storage. It still does not scan
— the environment is genuinely empty until "update()" or "add()" runs.

Staying in sync covers the refresh side in full.


"recreate=True" is not a reconnect
==================================

The direct constructor accepts "recreate=True" to replace the selected
state:

   env = OntoEnv(path=".demo-env", recreate=True, search_directories=["./brick"])

With managed storage, each call stages an empty replacement catalog
and any requested source scan, then publishes that replacement. Old
readers retain their versions. Cleanup in ".demo-env/.ontoenv-
snapshots/" retains current and previous publications plus all files
pinned by live views. Eligible files are reclaimed on writer startup,
successful publication or "env.prune()". Close the active writer
before recreating. Source files are untouched.

That is occasionally what you want, but it is not “open my
environment”. The non-destructive equivalent is:

   with OntoEnv.connect(".demo-env", search_directories=["./brick"]) as env:
       env.update()

And when you do mean the destructive version, the named form says so
out loud:

   env = OntoEnv.create(".demo-env", overwrite=True, search_directories=["./brick"])

One more constructor behavior worth knowing:
"OntoEnv(path="./project")" without "recreate" searches "./project"
*and its parents* for an existing managed environment directory, opens
what it finds, and raises "FileNotFoundError" otherwise. Convenient
interactively; too implicit for application code, where "connect" or
"open" name the path and the intent.

The constructor remains supported and is used internally. For new
code, the named methods are clearer.


Configuration on reopen
=======================

Settings persist with the environment. When you reopen it:

* **Omitting an option keeps the saved value.**

* **Passing a value overrides it** — including "False", ""default"",
  and "[]", which are real overrides rather than “unset”.

   OntoEnv.connect("./env")                        # everything as saved
   OntoEnv.connect("./env", strict=True)           # override strict, keep the rest
   OntoEnv.connect("./env", search_directories=[]) # explicitly clear search paths

Booleans are effectively tri-state on reopen: "None" preserves, "True"
and "False" both override. This applies to "strict", "offline",
"require_ontology_names", "use_cached_ontologies",
"remote_cache_ttl_secs", "resolution_policy", search directories, and
every filter list. "OntoEnv.open" behaves identically.

A writable connection saves overrides. A read-only one applies them to
that session only — a read-only worker cannot change what the writer
configured.

Changing configuration never triggers a scan. Runtime modes such as
"offline" and "strict" take effect immediately; changed discovery
paths and filters apply on the next "update()".

Managed graph and configuration edits publish before their methods
return. "flush()" flushes adapters and "close()" releases the handle;
neither adds a managed commit boundary. Rust callers can group edits
with "transaction". Existing views keep their captured version after
close.


How long should the object live?
================================

Keep the returned object in application state and reuse it:

   env = OntoEnv.connect("./ontology-env")
   try:
       # Startup has already loaded this ontology.
       view, members = env.get_closure("https://example.org/site")
       # Continue serving requests or running jobs with env.
   finally:
       env.close()  # Shutdown

Context managers provide the same cleanup for a shorter scope. Neither
form adds a managed commit boundary: writes publish before returning.
Returned views keep their captured version after "close".

A writable managed handle owns the single writer lock until close.
Read-only workers can remain open alongside it:

   reader = OntoEnv.open("./ontology-env", read_only=True)
   try:
       old = reader.snapshot()
       reader.refresh()  # Select another process's latest publication.
       current = reader.snapshot()
       # old and its returned views keep the original version.
   finally:
       reader.close()

Use live "env.get_*" graph reads for individual results. For several
reads that must agree, capture "env.snapshot()" and use its "view_*" /
"copy_*" methods. Reader "refresh" selects saved state; writer
"update" reads sources. See Use OntoEnv in a long-running service for
framework and multi-process patterns.


Removed constructor flags
=========================

The 0.7 API removes "create_or_use_cached" and "init_from_store". Use
"OntoEnv.connect(path)" to create or reopen an environment, and
"OntoEnv.adopt(path, store)" to catalog an existing external store.
For temporary stores, call "refresh_from_store(full=True)" explicitly.
Namespaces and prefix precedence
********************************

A prefix gives a namespace IRI a short name: "ex:ahu1" can stand for
"urn:example:ahu1" when "ex" is bound to "urn:example:". Changing a
binding changes how terms are displayed and how prefixed query names
are resolved. It does not rename the full IRIs in stored triples.

OntoEnv keeps ontology declarations and your saved prefix choices
separately. This lets you choose consistent names without editing
every ontology source.


Where bindings come from
========================

Within one ontology, SHACL "sh:declare" entries take precedence over
parser declarations such as Turtle "@prefix". Parser declarations are
captured when the source is parsed and saved in the catalog. Namespace
lookups use that saved metadata; they do not read files or fetch URLs.

Saved user bindings take precedence over both kinds of ontology
declaration. They resolve conflicts in two ways:

* If you bind an existing prefix to another namespace, your namespace
  wins.

* If you give an existing namespace a new prefix, the ontology’s other
  prefixes for that namespace are omitted from the merged mapping.

There is at most one saved user prefix for each namespace. Binding the
same namespace under another prefix removes its previous user binding.

Without a user binding, conflicting prefixes from different ontologies
are merged in traversal order, with later graphs winning. The order
across the whole environment is not guaranteed. Save a binding when
you need a stable choice.


Inspecting the effective mapping
================================

   from ontoenv import OntoEnv

   env = OntoEnv.connect("./ontology-env")
   env.get_namespaces()                       # all ontologies + saved bindings
   env.get_namespaces("urn:example:demo")      # one ontology + saved bindings
   env.get_namespaces("urn:example:demo", include_closure=True)
   env.get_bound_namespaces()                 # saved user bindings only

"get_closure()" and "get_union()" views carry the prefixes of their
selected graphs, plus all saved user bindings. An unrelated ontology’s
declarations are excluded from these views.

From the CLI, use "ontoenv namespaces --json" for the whole
environment, or "ontoenv namespaces <ontology-IRI> --closure --json"
for a closure.


Saving, changing, and removing a binding
========================================

In Python, these calls save changes immediately in the selected
version’s configuration for a writable persistent environment:

   env.bind_namespace("site", "urn:example:")
   assert env.get_bound_namespaces()["site"] == "urn:example:"

   # Pick a different name for the same namespace; "site" is removed.
   env.bind_namespace("building", "urn:example:")

   # Remove the saved choice and let ontology declarations apply again.
   removed = env.unbind_namespace("building")  # True if a binding existed

The equivalent CLI commands are:

   $ ontoenv config bind site urn:example:
   $ ontoenv config bind building urn:example:
   $ ontoenv config unbind building

Python returns "False" when unbinding an absent prefix; the CLI
reports an error. Removing a saved binding does not remove the
source’s declarations. The effective mapping can therefore contain
that prefix again afterward.

A read-only Python environment rejects these edits. A temporary
environment keeps them in memory only. Rust callers use
"bind_namespace" or "unbind_namespace" followed by "save_to_directory"
to persist changes.


Precedence when copying into rdflib
===================================

"env.copy_dataset()" creates a mutable rdflib dataset. You can also
pass an existing dataset to add the environment’s quads to it. Prefix
conflicts use this order:

1. Saved user bindings in the environment.

2. Existing bindings in the destination dataset, including rdflib
   defaults.

3. Ontology-declared prefixes.

A saved user binding replaces a conflicting destination prefix and
becomes the preferred prefix for its namespace. For example, saving
"schema -> urn:example:" makes the copy use "schema:ahu1" even though
rdflib normally reserves "schema" for "https://schema.org/".

Ontology declarations preserve the destination’s preferred bindings.
rdflib may assign a suffixed prefix such as "ex1" to resolve a
collision. This policy applies to "copy_dataset()"; it does not imply
that every "copy_*" graph method propagates the environment’s
bindings.


Bindings for one dataset or view
================================

Use rdflib’s "bind()" for a choice that belongs only to one dataset:

   dataset = env.get_dataset()
   dataset.bind("session", "urn:example:", override=True, replace=True)

This does not edit the environment configuration. A newly obtained
dataset uses the environment’s bindings. Calling
"env.refresh_dataset(dataset)" on a store-backed dataset also resets
its bindings from the environment, discarding local choices.

After "env.bind_namespace()" or "env.unbind_namespace()", obtain a new
dataset or view, or refresh an existing store-backed dataset, to see
the change. Existing copies keep their own bindings.

A "ViewGraph" supports "view.bind(prefix, namespace, override=True)"
for local changes. Its binding method has no "replace" argument; its
"override" flag controls replacement. The view’s prefixes take
precedence over rdflib defaults when the view is serialized.


Editing source declarations
===========================

After changing a source’s "@prefix" or "sh:declare" entries, call
"env.update()" to refresh source metadata. Use
"env.update(force=True)" to force re-parsing even if cache checks
consider the source unchanged. The CLI equivalent for a forced refresh
is "ontoenv update --all".

Existing catalogs created before parser prefixes were recorded report
only their SHACL declarations until sources are re-parsed. A forced
update fills in the parser prefixes. Saved user bindings still take
precedence after that update.

For command signatures and configuration fields, see CLI reference,
Python API reference, and Configuration.
Performance
***********

The 0.6 API separates catalog access from graph access, and views from
materialized graphs. Those choices have measurable consequences:
reopening an environment should depend on catalog size rather than RDF
triple count, while a view trades Python object allocation for a read-
only interface. This page states the measurements, their scope, and
the implementation details that produce them.


Summary of the benchmark
========================

* **Warm open took about 10 ms** for both one-graph catalogs tested,
  containing 1 and 124,000 triples respectively.

* **For the tested views,** SPARQL took less time than the in-memory
  rdflib baseline, full iteration took a similar amount of time, and
  individual triple lookups took more time.

In ordinary read paths, start with "get_*". Use "copy_*" where
mutation or the complete "rdflib.Graph" API is part of the
requirement.


Warm starts
===========

"python/bench_catalog_warm_start.py" adopts synthetic one-graph stores
holding 1 and 124,000 triples, then repeatedly reopens each catalog-
backed environment.

Both averaged about 10 ms per open — 9.75 ms and 9.95 ms — on an Apple
Silicon development machine, and neither warm loop ever called
"get_graph".

   cd python
   uv run python bench_catalog_warm_start.py

The near-identical result is consistent with the intended boundary:
warm-open cost tracks catalog records, not the size of the graphs they
describe. A warm open reads the catalog and does not call "get_graph".
This makes "connect" suitable for normal process startup; it does not
characterize the cost of later graph operations.


Views versus copies
===================

"python/bench_rdflib_store.py" loads Brick 1.4.4 and its imports
closure (15 graphs, ~237k triples) and times the same operations
across four "rdflib"-compatible backends:

"ontoenv-get"
   "env.get_closure(...)" — a read-only zero-copy view over the on-
   disk rdf5d store via "mmap", with in-memory permutation indexes.

"ontoenv-copy"
   "env.copy_closure(...)" — a mutable in-memory "rdflib.Graph"
   materialized from the same closure.

"rdflib-memory"
   The default rdflib "Memory" store, loaded from the same triples.

"oxigraph"
   The "oxrdflib" store, loaded from the same triples. Optional;
   skipped if "oxrdflib" is not installed.

   cd python
   uv run python bench_rdflib_store.py \
       --brick https://brickschema.org/schema/1.4.4/Brick.ttl \
       --repeat 3

   # Or point at a local file for offline runs:
   uv run python bench_rdflib_store.py --brick ../brick/Brick.ttl


Results
=======

The table reports the lower time from two runs on an Apple Silicon
laptop. Absolute times depend on hardware, RDF input, query shape, and
dependency versions. The results apply to this dataset and these
workloads.

+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Workload             | ontoenv-get          | ontoenv-copy         | rdflib-memory        | oxigraph             |
|======================|======================|======================|======================|======================|
| Iterate all triples  | **131 ms**           | 154 ms               | 135 ms               | 784 ms               |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Match "?s            | 0.07 ms              | 0.04 ms              | 0.04 ms              | 0.13 ms              |
| owl:imports ?o"      |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Match                | 0.12 ms              | 0.05 ms              | 0.05 ms              | 0.25 ms              |
| "brick:Equipment ?p  |                      |                      |                      |                      |
| ?o"                  |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Match "?s ?p         | 1.53 ms              | 1.48 ms              | 1.33 ms              | 5.02 ms              |
| owl:Class"           |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| SPARQL "COUNT" of    | **1.41 ms**          | 114 ms               | 110 ms               | 5.30 ms              |
| "rdf:type"           |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| SPARQL               | **0.57 ms**          | 4.46 ms              | 4.32 ms              | 0.47 ms              |
| "rdfs:subClassOf*"   |                      |                      |                      |                      |
| of "brick:Equipment" |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| SPARQL "SELECT ...   | **5.48 ms**          | 10.99 ms             | 10.52 ms             | 5.50 ms              |
| rdfs:label ... LIMIT |                      |                      |                      |                      |
| 1000"                |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+

Bold marks measurements where "ontoenv-get" was lower than the
"rdflib-memory" baseline.

Measurements cover steady-state reads. Backend construction — view
creation, closure materialization, loading the reference stores —
happens before the timed region, and each workload gets one untimed
warm-up. If startup or one-shot export latency is your actual
question, measure that end to end instead.


Reading the results
===================

**``ontoenv-copy`` ≈ ``rdflib-memory`` everywhere.** "copy_closure"
materializes into a vanilla rdflib "Memory" store, so it inherits the
same query engine and the same profile. The timed region excludes the
earlier materialization step.

**The view had lower times for the SPARQL queries with small result
sets.** The whole query plan runs against the rdf5d-backed dataset via
"spareval", joining on integer term IDs and never crossing the FFI
boundary for individual triples. "COUNT rdf:type" took 1.4 ms through
the view and 110 ms through in-memory rdflib. The "LIMIT 1000" label
scan took 5.5 ms and 10.5 ms respectively.

**Full iteration matches in-memory.** 131 ms vs 135 ms across ~237k
triples. The all-unbound path streams directly from the snapshot’s
term-ID iterator with a u64-keyed cache for Python terms, building no
intermediate term objects per row.

**Microsecond lookups still favour rdflib.** "owl:imports" matching is
0.07 ms as a view against 0.04 ms in memory. The in-memory
implementation can answer this pattern with a dictionary lookup. If
that is your dominant access pattern, benchmark it directly.

**Oxigraph had similar times for two of the SPARQL workloads.** In
this benchmark, its load and full-iteration times were higher. If one
dataset serves many queries, measure the complete workload, including
loading and concurrency.


Implementation details affecting the results
============================================

**Permutation indexes.** Binding an rdf5d snapshot eagerly builds four
posting-list indexes, held in memory for the life of the snapshot:

* "PSO" and "POS" for a **bound predicate**

* "SPO" for a **bound subject** with unbound predicate

* "OSP" for a **bound object** with unbound predicate

A triple pattern with any bound term reads the matching posting list
instead of scanning every triple in every graph of the closure. Only
the fully unbound pattern scans directly.

The builds run in parallel threads at bind time — tens of milliseconds
per permutation for the Brick closure — so the cost lands once, up
front, rather than on the first query of each pattern shape. Because
an index is built from the snapshot you just opened, there is nothing
to invalidate: no staleness checks, no sidecar files. Older versions
wrote a "store.r5tu.idx" sidecar; it is unused now and removed on the
next flush.

The indexes cost roughly a few times the on-disk snapshot’s size in
RAM, and are discarded when the snapshot drops. There is no
configuration.

**Property-path closure rewriting.** The query layer also precomputes,
in memory and lazily on first use, the transitive closure of three
predicates: "rdfs:subClassOf", "rdfs:subPropertyOf", and "owl:sameAs".

At query time the evaluator intercepts "?x P+ ?y" and "?x P* ?y"
patterns whose predicate is in that list and substitutes a
materialized "VALUES" block before handing the query to spareval.
Supported shapes: "P+", "P*", "^P+", "^P*" for a single IRI "P". That
is why "subClassOf*" runs in 0.57 ms against 4.32 ms for in-memory
rdflib.

The rewrite bails out — leaving the path for spareval to evaluate
normally — when the predicate is not in the precomputed list, when the
path is a sequence, alternative, or negated property set rather than a
direct "P+"/"P*" of one IRI, or when both endpoints of the path are
variables.

   from ontoenv import OntoEnv

   # Permutation indexes are built when the rdf5d snapshot is bound.
   env = OntoEnv.connect("./ontology-env")
   env.add("https://brickschema.org/schema/1.4.4/Brick.ttl")
   env.flush()

   # The property-closure table stays lazy: the first supported path query
   # builds it, and later queries reuse it.
   view, _ = env.get_closure("https://brickschema.org/schema/1.4/Brick")


Rules of thumb
==============

* Use "get_*" to keep memory low, for SPARQL returning small result
  sets ("COUNT", aggregations, "LIMIT"), and where code must not
  mutate the environment.

* Use "copy_*" when mutation or an API exclusive to "rdflib.Graph" is
  required.

* For the supported recursive property paths, benchmark "get_*" first;
  the closure table specifically accelerates those shapes.

* For an application serving many queries from one loaded dataset,
  compare Oxigraph under representative load and concurrency.
Publication validation and acceptance gates
*******************************************

Status: storage release candidate, October 23, 2026. The measurements
below were taken on the publisher before its default Rust/Python/CLI
integration. They describe synthetic fixtures, not production
performance SLOs or a proof of durability on every local filesystem.
The publication protocol remains the same in 0.7.0-rc.1; application
integration has separate regression coverage.


Platform correctness
====================

The held-open CURRENT regression and the complete feature suite passed
on Linux, macOS and Windows at Rust 1.88 for commit "ac607d9". Both
Windows jobs also passed ten repetitions of the three-reader/twenty-
publication stress test. The original failure was real: tempfile’s
MoveFileExW-only replacement returned access denied while readers were
active. "std::fs::rename" uses a Windows POSIX-semantics fallback,
allowing old handles to retain their bytes while new opens select the
replacement. No sleeps or permission-error suppression were added to
publication.

All cooperating writers still require the stable writer lock. The
tests do not authorize concurrent external replacement or truncation
of mapped graph files.


Accepted Windows release scope
==============================

Decision recorded October 25, 2026: Windows 0.7 ships coherent
publication, owned read views and process-crash recovery with **best-
effort power-loss durability**. A power failure may require rebuilding
the environment from ontology sources. A successful commit or
retention of a previous version does not guarantee that a complete
version remains recoverable after power loss. Existing flushing is
preserved; directory syncing remains unsupported on Windows. The
process-exit CI coverage and the Linux guest results below do not
strengthen this Windows contract. See the snapshot guide.


Guest crash durability
======================

The disposable QEMU harness completed a nine-case pilot followed by
**27 cases across three repeated cycles**. It used a 64 MiB ext4
image, a Linux 7.2.6-76070206-generic guest, QEMU 8.2.2 with TCG and
"cache=none", and a small ontology/configuration/alias fixture in an
already initialized environment. The host SIGKILLed QEMU at the
selected publication boundary, then booted a fresh guest. Verification
mounted the filesystem read-only after ext4’s journal recovery and
opened only "SnapshotReader", before any application recovery writer.

+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Crash boundary                    | Required result                   | Three-cycle result                |
|===================================|===================================|===================================|
| Object ready; manifest            | Old version                       | Old version in every case         |
| written/synced/directory synced;  |                                   |                                   |
| pointer written/synced            |                                   |                                   |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| CURRENT replaced, parent          | Complete old or new version       | Old version in all three cases    |
| directory not yet synced          |                                   |                                   |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Parent directory synced           | New version                       | New version in all three cases    |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Public commit returned success    | New version                       | New version in all three cases    |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+

Every reopened version had matching graph data, configuration revision
and alias state. The pre-directory-sync result demonstrates why atomic
visibility alone does not establish durable publication. Keep the
final directory barrier.

This establishes a bounded **guest kernel/page-cache-loss test** for
this filesystem/kernel setup. The host and physical device caches were
not power-cycled. It does not cover every torn/reordered device write,
initialization interruptions, large-store crash cases, other
filesystems or Windows/macOS power-loss semantics. Directory sync
remains a no-op on Windows. Normal-operation and process-exit
correctness there must not be advertised as the same durability
guarantee as this Linux experiment.

Reproduction instructions are in "lib/tests/support/README.md"; the
machine-readable report is "docs/reviews/snapshot-durability-
vm-2026-10-23.json". Guest serial logs and disk images remain in the
local "/tmp" artifact directory identified by that report. The harness
exposes no host directories, network or physical disks.


Workload measurements
=====================

The release diagnostic uses local, offline synthetic sources with long
hashed literals. Four active reader processes repeatedly query their
retained version while the writer makes three separate one-graph
commits, followed by one alias-only commit. Readers then refresh and
build a new PSO index while retaining their old snapshot/index. A
burst staged in one update would have one publication; this experiment
deliberately measures three separate publications.

Five fresh-process warm reads were measured per size. The first
selective query builds the PSO index; warm selective queries reuse it.
A per-file eviction request was also made, but POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED is
advisory and does not prove cold storage reads. No host-global cache
clearing was performed.

+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Measurement               | 100 graphs / 13.9 MiB     | 100 graphs / 19.5 MiB     | 200 graphs / 55.8 MiB     |
|===========================|===========================|===========================|===========================|
| Warm open, median         | 11.5 ms                   | 15.9 ms                   | 68.0 ms                   |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Open after advisory       | 16.1 ms                   | 22.8 ms                   | 79.9 ms                   |
| eviction request          |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| First graph copy, warm    | 0.71 ms                   | 0.96 ms                   | 2.52 ms                   |
| median                    |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| First indexed query,      | 26 ms                     | 39 ms                     | 158 ms                    |
| warm-file median          |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Three graph-changing      | 230–270 ms                | 400–440 ms                | 1,039–1,142 ms            |
| commits, range            |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Metadata-only commit      | 63 ms                     | 25 ms                     | 24 ms                     |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Reader refresh, median    | 26 ms                     | 36 ms                     | 104 ms                    |
| across four processes     |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| First indexed query after | 37 ms                     | 57 ms                     | 168 ms                    |
| refresh, median           |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Writer peak RSS during    | 124 MiB                   | 178 MiB                   | 421 MiB                   |
| update burst              |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Four readers’ aggregate   | 128 MiB                   | 204 MiB                   | 472 MiB                   |
| PSS, one indexed version  |                           |                           |                           |
| each                      |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Four readers’ aggregate   | 245 MiB                   | 392 MiB                   | 960 MiB                   |
| PSS, retaining old and    |                           |                           |                           |
| new indexed versions      |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
| Retained RDF5D bytes      | 55.6 MiB                  | 77.9 MiB                  | 223.0 MiB                 |
| after three graph commits |                           |                           |                           |
| and an alias commit       |                           |                           |                           |
+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+

Held-reader sampled query p95 was approximately 0.039, 0.047 and 0.127
ms respectively. The maximum observed query was 0.68, 0.36 and 8.9 ms.
Those samples span the ready-to-refresh interval, including setup
around the writer burst; percentiles use each reader’s first 4,096
timings, while maxima cover every query. They are not production tail-
latency bounds. Results are single diagnostic runs per fixture and
include normal scheduler/storage variation.

RSS includes shared mappings in each process; aggregate PSS apportions
shared pages. These measurements include one permutation index, not
every possible query index. Memory under more query shapes or more
retained versions can be higher. Logical retained-file lengths exclude
filesystem allocation overhead.

The source, commands, process reports and hashes are retained in
"docs/reviews/snapshot-workload-2026-10-23.json". The worker and
controller are "lib/examples/snapshot_workload.rs" and
"lib/tests/support/snapshot_workload.py".


Proposed gates before normal API integration
============================================

These are historical engineering targets from before integration.
Current memory measurements are advisory, not release limits. The
accepted Windows contract above supersedes any stronger implication
from these proposed gates; the power-loss campaign applies only to its
tested Linux configuration.

Correctness gates are strict: no mixed versions, no failed cooperating
publications under the tested concurrent-reader workload, retained
views stay unchanged, and failed refresh preserves the old view.
Acknowledged commits must survive the defined durability campaign; a
single loss or incomplete selected version fails that gate. Keep
platform durability claims tied to tested/specified flush behavior.

For initial engineering work at roughly 20 MiB with four active
readers, use these **provisional budgets**, subject to
workload/product review:

* Graph-changing commit: under one second in the diagnostic workload.

* Refresh: under 100 ms, plus under 100 ms for the first selective
  query/index.

* Writer peak RSS: under 256 MiB; reader peak RSS under 128 MiB for
  one indexed version and under 256 MiB when deliberately retaining
  two.

* Retention: continue to expose/document full-store growth per graph-
  changing commit. Do not enable automatic deletion without a process-
  safe reader protocol.

The target fixture fits these provisional budgets; the larger fixture
crosses some of them. They are not new public latency/memory promises
or statistically validated p95 thresholds. Revisit them with real
ontology/query workloads before making the new publisher the default
or expanding its supported durability scope.


Ownership follow-up and initial Rust integration
================================================

The focused ownership review found no cycle requiring a new release
mechanism. Weak-reference tests check that ordinary refresh frees
unreferenced old metadata and RDF5D snapshots, while owned query
iterators retain their RDF backing until dropped. Cloned handles share
a snapshot, and metadata-only refresh now preserves the same mapped
RDF5D object and its whole-store indexes. Scoped View indexes remain
view-local to preserve scope-specific property-path semantics.

A paired ~19.5 MiB run with four active readers confirms the
difference between ordinary refresh and intentionally retaining
history:

+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Reader behavior      | Aggregate PSS before | Aggregate PSS after  | Refresh median       | New index/query      |
|                      |                      |                      |                      | median               |
|======================|======================|======================|======================|======================|
| Keep old and new     | 204 MiB              | 392 MiB              | 36 ms                | 57 ms                |
| indexed versions     |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| Release old view     | 204 MiB              | 204 MiB              | 57 ms                | 47 ms                |
| before refresh       |                      |                      |                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+

Ordinary refresh includes destruction of the old state; retained-view
refresh defers that work. All four release-mode workers confirmed the
old RDF snapshot was destroyed before building the new index. File
retention remains unchanged. This is one diagnostic run per mode with
independent equivalent fixtures, not a controlled latency/memory
guarantee. Raw worker reports, commands and hashes are in
"docs/reviews/snapshot-ownership-2026-10-23.json".

The initial explicit integration added "OntoEnv::create_snapshot",
"OntoEnv::open_snapshot" and "OntoEnv::open_snapshot_writer",
returning specialized reader/writer handles. The 0.7 release candidate
additionally uses the publisher through the normal Rust, Python and
CLI APIs, including recursive source updates, explicit migration and
independently owned Python query views. Regression tests cover nested
rollback/unwinding, bounded imports, coherent reader refresh,
recreation, in-flight dataset iterators, copied roots and release
upgrades. A writer-lock guard explicitly unlocks before closing so
inherited descriptors from concurrent process spawning cannot prolong
a dropped writer’s lock.

Avoid implicit refresh of retained views: their stable identity is the
consistency guarantee. Per-graph disk COW would not directly remove
per-process in-memory query indexes and is not justified by these
measurements alone. Safe online file cleanup remains future work.


Default backend release candidate
=================================

The 0.7.0-rc.1 integration passed local validation on October 23,
2026:

* "cargo test --workspace --release --offline": **240 passed**,
  including doctests; seven process helpers/examples remained
  intentionally ignored.

* "cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --offline --
  -D warnings" and "cargo fmt --all -- --check": passed.

* The release abi3 wheel built successfully; its complete Python 3.14
  suite passed **165 tests**. The 21 warnings were existing
  deprecation warnings from rdflib and compatibility APIs. The
  pyontoenv shim import test also passed.

* A fresh environment created by the released **0.5.5** wheel migrated
  through the new wheel. Stored triples survived, legacy file contents
  remained intact, and ordinary open refused the old format before
  explicit migration.

* Sphinx rebuilt with warnings treated as errors; workspace version
  checks and diff whitespace checks passed.

The additional tests exercise ordinary import/update/rename
publication, configuration changes with deliberately bounded imports,
rollback and unwinding, reader refresh, retained graph/closure/dataset
views, explicit dataset rebinding with an outstanding iterator,
migration/recovery, copied publication roots, logical recreation, and
config/reset root selection through "ONTOENV_DIR". Staged graph
contents are shared through "Arc" across nested checkpoints and
publication preparation; graph-copy APIs still allocate their
requested copies.

These local results do not replace the Linux/macOS/Windows CI matrix
for the new default integration. The earlier VM crash and workload
measurements above exercise the underlying publisher, not the complete
new API facade. No new power-loss or performance guarantee is inferred
from the integration tests.
Staying in sync
***************


Managed reader refresh
======================

With the 0.7 managed backend, "env.refresh()" selects the latest
complete publication. It reads no ontology sources and does not wait
for a live writer. Until refresh, the reader retains its original
catalog, configuration and RDF. Old returned snapshots and query views
keep their original versions after a refresh. A failed refresh
preserves the previous selection. See OntoEnv publication and
snapshots and Migrate to the 0.7 storage backend.


Source updates and custom stores
================================

OntoEnv has a saved view of the world, and the world moves. Files get
edited, remote ontologies get republished, and — if you supplied your
own graph store — something else may write into that store directly.

There are two reconciliation operations, and they solve genuinely
different problems.

+----------------------------+---------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
|                            | "env.update()"                        | "env.refresh_from_store()"            |
|============================|=======================================|=======================================|
| Reconciles                 | Ontology **sources**: files and URLs  | Graphs changed **directly in a custom |
|                            |                                       | store**                               |
+----------------------------+---------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| Reads                      | The filesystem and the network        | Your "graph_store" object             |
+----------------------------+---------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| Follows "owl:imports"      | Yes                                   | No                                    |
+----------------------------+---------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| Relevant when              | Always                                | Only with "graph_store="              |
+----------------------------+---------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+

Both exist because they answer different questions. “Has "site.ttl"
changed on disk, and if so what does it import now?” is not the same
question as “did another process write into my database while I wasn’t
looking?” Collapsing them into one call would mean every restart
either checks the network or scans your whole backend.


Refreshing sources
==================

   env.update()                                  # changed files + expired remotes
   env.update(force=True)                        # every known source, regardless
   env.update("https://example.org/site.ttl")    # one source
   env.update("https://example.org/site.ttl", force=True)

"update()" checks the configured search directories for new, changed,
and removed files, and re-fetches remote ontologies whose cached
copies have outlived the TTL. It follows "owl:imports" throughout, so
dependencies stay current along with the ontologies that pulled them
in.

With a location argument it updates that one source and replaces its
stored graph, again following imports.

Whether "update" touches the network at all depends on the
environment’s "offline" and cache settings. See Work offline and
control caching.


Why connect doesn’t do this for you
===================================

Because reading files and fetching URLs is expensive, and startup is
exactly when you least want to pay for it.

A service that restarts under load would otherwise re-parse every
ontology on every restart. Keeping "update()" explicit means the cost
is scheduled by you — at deploy time, on a timer, from an admin
endpoint — rather than imposed by the library.


Reconciling a custom store
==========================

This section only matters if you passed "graph_store=".

Changes made **through** "env" update your store and OntoEnv’s catalog
together; nothing extra is needed. Changes made **directly to the
store** are different, because OntoEnv did not see them happen.

How much OntoEnv can do about that depends entirely on what your store
can tell it:

**The store reports per-graph revisions** ("graph_revisions()").
OntoEnv rereads only the graphs that actually changed. This is the
good case, and the reason that optional method is worth implementing.

**The store reports that it changed, but not which graphs**
("store_state()" only). OntoEnv raises rather than guessing, and asks
you to request "sync="full"" explicitly.

**The store reports nothing.** OntoEnv trusts its saved catalog until
you ask for a refresh.

That middle case is a deliberate design choice. "sync="auto"" will
never silently turn a normal restart into a full scan of your database
— if the only correct action is expensive, you get to decide when to
pay for it.

   report = env.refresh_from_store()                    # incremental
   report = env.refresh_from_store(graphs=[iri, ...])   # exactly these
   report = env.refresh_from_store(full=True)           # forget and rebuild

   print(report.added, report.changed, report.removed)


Targeted refreshes are exact
============================

"graphs=" is an exact set of backend graph IDs. OntoEnv does not
expand it — if you name a root, you get the root, not its imports. To
refresh a root along with the closure already recorded for it, compose
the two calls:

   report = env.refresh_from_store(graphs=env.list_closure(root))

That works when a known closure was rewritten together. But if the
external edit introduced a *new* imported graph, that graph is not in
the old closure yet, so a targeted refresh will not see it. An
incremental refresh finds it when the store reports per-graph changes;
otherwise "full=True" is the answer.

A targeted refresh also says nothing about graphs it did not look at.
The report lists those as still pending, and a later connection will
still detect that the store and the catalog have drifted.


Synchronization at connect time
===============================

"sync=" controls the same machinery during "connect":

""auto"" (default)
   Create or index on first use, reuse the saved catalog on restart,
   incorporate external changes when the store can identify them.
   Never reads ontology sources.

""full""
   Reread every graph in the store. For known out-of-band changes the
   store cannot identify.

""catalog""
   Use the saved catalog without reading graph contents at all. For
   controlled deployments where another part of the system guarantees
   the saved view is correct.

None of these fetch ontology sources. After connecting, call
"update()" when files and URLs should be refreshed too.


When commits are interrupted
============================

A mutation writes graphs, then publishes the updated catalog. If a
process dies between those steps, a "catalog.pending" marker remains
and the next open raises "CatalogRecoveryError" rather than trusting a
catalog that might not describe every graph.

Normal completed mutations remove the marker as part of their commit —
including best-effort ones. In non-strict mode,
"import_dependencies(..., fetch_missing=True)" and
"get_dependencies(..., fetch_missing=True)" may skip imports they
cannot reach, but the partial result they *did* commit is a complete,
valid commit. So a recovery marker always means an interrupted or
failed write, never merely a missing import.

See Recover an interrupted environment.
OntoEnv publication and snapshots
*********************************

Starting with 0.7.0-rc.1, immutable publication is the default storage
backend for new managed persistent environments in Rust, Python and
the CLI. It is always compiled, without a feature flag. Temporary
environments and caller-provided graph stores retain their existing
behavior and their backend’s transaction guarantees.

Publication coordinates an OntoEnv catalog, configuration and
immutable RDF5D artifact. RDF5D remains the file builder and query
engine. OntoEnv implements writer exclusion, commit and refresh with
immutable JSON manifests and an atomic "CURRENT" file, without a
database dependency. See the design review and validation report for
the protocol and measured limits.

Existing ".ontoenv/" environments require explicit migration.
Migration copies the stored RDF and metadata, retains the original
files, and publishes the new directory only after validation. Earlier
redb-based prototype environments are rejected without automatic
conversion.


Try it
======

   cargo run -p ontoenv --example transactional_snapshots
   cargo test -p ontoenv --lib --test test_snapshots --test test_concurrency

The example keeps a writer open, opens a reader, publishes new graph
content and an alias, then refreshes the reader. A retained old query
view still reads the old generation.

   use ontoenv::{SnapshotReader, SnapshotWriter};

   let mut writer = SnapshotWriter::create(config)?;
   let mut update = writer.begin_update();
   let id = update.add_from_bytes(location, bytes, format)?;
   update.add_alias("urn:alias", id.name().as_str())?;
   let committed = update.commit()?;

   let mut reader = SnapshotReader::open(root)?;
   let old = reader.snapshot();
   let old_view = old.view_graph(&id)?;
   // Further writer commits do not change `old` or reader.snapshot().
   reader.refresh()?;

These explicit entry points return "SnapshotWriter" and
"SnapshotReader". "SnapshotWriter::open(root)" opens an existing
writer. Normal "OntoEnv::connect/create/open" also use this backend,
with the existing source and import pipeline. Their successful graph
and configuration mutations publish before returning. "env.snapshot()"
captures the selected committed version; "env.refresh()" advances a
managed read handle without reading sources. Rust callers can group
operations with "env.transaction(|env| { ...; Ok(()) })"; nested
errors and unwinding restore staged graphs, catalog, configuration and
runtime settings.

Python uses the same lifecycle:

   from ontoenv import OntoEnv

   writer = OntoEnv.connect("./env", offline=True)
   writer.add("./ontology.ttl")
   reader = OntoEnv.open("./env", read_only=True)
   old = reader.snapshot()
   dataset = old.view_dataset()
   print(old.info)  # environment ID, generation, parent, committed_at, opened_at
   writer.update()
   reader.refresh()  # select a complete newer version, if one exists
   # old, dataset and previously returned graph/closure views keep their version.
   reader.close()
   writer.close()

"EnvironmentSnapshot" provides "get_ontology_names()",
"get_ontologies()", paired "view_*"/"copy_*" queries, namespace
access, a copied "config" dictionary and "info". These handles remain
usable after the environment closes. "OntoEnv.read_snapshot(path)"
opens one owned version without retaining a live environment. A Python
snapshot supports "close()", "closed", and "with":

   with OntoEnv.read_snapshot("./ontology-env") as version:
       graph = version.view_graph("urn:example:ontology")
   # The version handle is closed. The escaped graph still owns its backing.
   print(len(graph))
   del graph  # Releases this view's ownership; later cleanup can reclaim its file.
